analysis.one_liner: Lifts the Social Security payroll tax cap so all earnings are taxed, and boosts annual cost-of-living increases for seniors.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in July 2025 with 2 Democratic cosponsors and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it has seen no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: Today, wages above a set amount (about $176,100 in 2025) are exempt from Social Security payroll taxes. This bill would phase that exemption out between 2026 and 2031, so that after 2031 every dollar of earnings is taxed to fund Social Security. It would also count very high earnings in the benefit formula, though at very low rates, and it would switch the annual cost-of-living adjustment to an index that tracks prices seniors actually face, typically producing larger raises.
analysis.who_benefits: Social Security beneficiaries, who would get cost-of-living raises more closely matched to their spending on health care and housing, and the program itself, which would gain a large new source of revenue that helps extend the trust fund's solvency. Low-income seniors would also be protected from losing Medicaid or SSI benefits because of a larger Social Security check.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Social Security beneficiaries and the program

how_it_helps.text: The bill phases out the taxable maximum so that Social Security payroll taxes apply to all earnings after 2031, adding revenue that helps keep benefits payable, and it revises the benefit formula to give high earners some credit for the extra taxes they pay.

Cost-of-living adjustments would be calculated using a new Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers, reflecting the spending habits of people 62 and older, whose costs (especially medical care) typically rise faster than the general index.

Any benefit increase from the new cost-of-living formula could not be counted as income when determining eligibility for Medicaid or Supplemental Security Income, so low-income seniors would not lose those benefits because their Social Security check went up.

analysis.who_pays: The roughly top earners with wages or self-employment income above the current cap (about $176,100 in 2025). They, and their employers, would pay the combined 12.4% Social Security tax on earnings above the cap during the phase-out and on all earnings after 2031. High earners would receive only modest extra benefits in return, because the bill credits surplus earnings at very low rates.
analysis.who_pays_short: High earners above the wage cap

drawbacks.text: Workers and self-employed people earning above the cap would pay the full Social Security tax on all their earnings, but the benefit formula credits those surplus earnings at only 3% and then 0.25% — far below the rates applied to ordinary wages — so high earners would pay far more in taxes than they would get back, making the tax much less of an insurance contribution for them.

Larger cost-of-living increases from the seniors' price index would raise federal outlays faster than under the current formula, adding pressure on the program's finances even as the new tax revenue helps offset it.

A payroll tax increase on high earners, including on the employer side, is the standard objection opponents raise: it is a direct tax increase that critics argue could discourage high-skilled work or business activity in high-tax states.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The trade is simple and deliberately one-sided: a large new tax on the highest earners buys more generous, more secure Social Security benefits for everyone else, including the roughly 90% of workers whose earnings are already fully taxed. The benefit increases for high earners are token-level, so this functions as a transfer from top earners to the program and its beneficiaries. The main design question is timing — the tax phase-out starts in 2026 while the seniors' cost-of-living index arrives later — but the core exchange is clear.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late July 2025 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it has sat without a hearing, a markup, or any vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Mazie Hirono introduced the bill on July 31, 2025, with Sens. Tina Smith and Jeff Merkley as cosponsors.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; no further action has been taken since.
Only 2 of 45 Senate Democrats have cosponsored the bill, and no Republicans have signed on.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High earners above the payroll tax cap, who continue to pay Social Security tax only on their first ~$176,100 of earnings, and the current benefit and cost-of-living formulas remain unchanged.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners keep the tax cap

for.name: Sen. Mazie Hirono
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its introduction

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: The committee with jurisdiction over Social Security and payroll taxes
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and both cosponsors are Democrats (2 of 45 Senate Democrats); no Republican support is visible in the record, and the bill has not reached a vote where partisan breakdowns could be measured.

industries.industry: High earners with wages above the cap
industries.note: They would pay the 12.4% combined Social Security tax on all earnings during and after the phase-out, while receiving only marginal extra benefits. Their financial interest lies in keeping the current cap, which costs the program revenue.

industries.industry: High-earning self-employed professionals and business owners
industries.note: Self-employed people pay both the employee and employer halves of the payroll tax, so the full 12.4% rate would apply to their income above the cap.
They would get cost-of-living increases tied to a seniors' price index, typically larger than the general index, with protection for Medicaid and SSI eligibility.

analysis.trajectory: Bills to lift the payroll tax cap are introduced nearly every Congress and almost never reach the Senate floor. With no Republican cosponsors, only 2 Democratic cosponsors, and no committee action months after referral, the realistic outlook is that this bill dies in the Finance Committee when this Congress ends in January 2027.
